lines.text: Jackrabbit comes out of SnapSpace with the small shudder you have learned to brace for, and then nothing. No traffic control. No docking lights. Prometheus Station hangs against the stars as a darker patch of dark, picked out by a handful of navigation beacons still blinking out of habit.

That was a clean transition, Jack. Better than clean. You held station to within a centimetre a second before the strands went out, which is why we didn’t feel it. I’d like you to notice that, because in about four minutes you’re going to be too busy to notice anything.
Four minutes?

There’s no welcome. No automated hail, no transponder handshake, no thermal signature from the reactor. Either Prometheus is dead or it is pretending very hard. I lean towards dead. I’m sorry. I know what you were hoping to find here.
You were hoping to find your parents. Not them, exactly. The paper trail of them. The reason a mining couple on Alpha-7 had a name that turned up, decades later, in a research station’s records.

choices.text: “What do you make of the silence?”

lines.text: Honestly? It frightens me a little. A station this size doesn’t go quiet by accident. Somebody decommissioned it, and they were thorough: I can’t raise a single maintenance node, and maintenance nodes are built to survive almost anything. Whoever left, they didn’t want to be followed.
I say this so you know what I think, not to stop you. I’d rather be frightened with you than careful without you. Shall we go in?
We go in.

The docking collar takes you on the third attempt, grudgingly, like a door that has forgotten how. Inside, the air is thin and cold and smells of nothing at all. Emergency lighting makes a corridor out of the dark.

I have the station’s skeleton: power routing, pressure doors, the layout. I don’t have its memory. Every data core I can reach has been wiped, and not the lazy way. Someone overwrote them, then overwrote the overwriting. That’s a corporate habit. It costs money to be that careful.

Two places might still hold something. The archive core on the research level, which was wiped but might have a cache nobody knew about. Or the maintenance bays, where things get labelled by people who don’t read the security memos.
The archive core is a cathedral of dead racks. You walk the aisles with a hand lamp while Aggie talks you through what each block used to be, as if introducing you to people who have left the room.

Nothing. Nothing. Nothing. Wait. Third rack from the end, the one with the cracked housing. That’s a cache controller. It was never on the main index, so whoever wiped the index never knew to wipe it. Pull the module for me, would you? Gently. It’s older than you are.
The module gives up a few hundred fragments. Most are noise. One is a parts record, and it has words in it you recognise.

The maintenance bays are a mess, which is encouraging. Nobody wipes a mess. Crates stand half-packed where someone was interrupted. A hand-written tag hangs from a cradle built for something the size of a chair.
Read me the tag? My optics in here are terrible and I don’t trust the light.
“QFM test article. Return to V.R. by courier only. Do not SnapMesh.”
QFM. Quantum Flux Modulator. Jack, that’s a component of the Starling device. And ‘V.R.’ is Vectarion Research. I know that name. Give me a moment to be sure how I know it.

Here’s what I have, and I’ll give you all of it. Vectarion Research was a QuantumGrid subsidiary, wound up years ago, on paper. Prometheus built or tested a Quantum Flux Modulator for them, which means the Starling technology didn’t die with the Dyson Array. It went somewhere, and it went by hand.

Every shipping stub in this place carries the same carrier mark. Aletheion Logistics. Not a Consortium giant, a specialist. Couriers. By the look of it, Vectarion used nobody else, ever. If the trail to your family runs through Vectarion, it runs through Aletheion’s cargo bays.
You turn the tag over in your hands. Thirteen years old, in a dead station, holding the first solid thing you have ever found.
Then that’s where we go.
Go how? Aletheion doesn’t sell tickets. You can’t walk into a courier company and ask to see their old manifests.
No. But they hire pilots.
The silence that follows is not one of her pauses. It is the sound of an intelligence running a very large number of outcomes.

I’m going to tell you everything I think, and then it’s your decision. One: you are thirteen. Two: you are the best pilot I have ever flown with, and I flew with Agatha Locke’s test crews. Three: a corporate courier system watches its people the way a mine watches its workers, but with better cameras. Four: if it worked, it would put you inside the only organisation that knows where Starling went.

Five, and this is the one I keep coming back to: it would take years. Not weeks. You would have to become someone else for years, and I would have to help you do it. I don’t know what that does to a person. I don’t know what it does to us.

choices.text: “What would you do, if it were you?”

lines.text: If it were me? Agatha told me to survive at all costs, and I have spent a long time learning that ‘at all costs’ is not the same as ‘at any cost’. I would go. I would go in with my eyes open, and I would make sure the person I went in with knew that I’d tell them the moment it stopped being worth it.
That’s a promise, by the way. Whatever we find in there, I’ll tell you. All of it, as soon as I know it. That’s the one thing I can give you that they can’t take.
Then we’d better do it properly.
Back aboard Jackrabbit, with Prometheus shrinking in the aft display, Aggie builds you a face.

Look at the main display. That’s you, as far as any Aletheion system will ever know. The jaw a little more defined. Lines at the eyes that say ‘experience’ rather than ‘thirteen’. I’ve deepened your voice on every channel I’ll be handling, which will be all of them. Jack Abbott, nineteen, licensed pilot, raised on an outpost that keeps no records worth checking.
You kept my name.

Deliberately. A person answering to a false name hesitates for a fraction of a second, every time, and a fraction of a second is exactly what corporate security is trained to notice. Hesitation is a tell, Jack. Remember that. It’ll matter more than you think.
You will remember it. Not for the reason she means.
Application submitted. Now we wait, and while we wait, you practise walking like someone who has never once had to hide from a guard.
